results.summary:
There are many devils in the details:
- Prerequisites are not always implicitly practiced, so you really need two graphs: not only a prerequisite graph for extending students' knowledge frontiers forward using mastery learning, but also an "encompassing" graph for propagating the right amount of credit backwards using spaced repetition. (A topic "encompasses" a simpler topic if the simpler topic is implicitly practiced as a component skill.)
- Like the prerequisite graph, the encompassing graph has to be encoded by a domain expert. I've personally encoded tens of thousands of encompassing records over the years. (Our curriculum director manages the prerequisite graph; I manage the encompassing graph.)
- Implicit repetitions need to be discounted appropriately: they are often too early to count for full credit towards the encompassed topic's next repetition.
- Ecompassings are often fractional: component skills are often practiced only in part as opposed to in full.

- To account for these details I had to formalize a novel theory of maximum-efficiency spaced repetition in hierarchical knowledge structures. It's called Fractional Implicit Repetition (FIRe). I also developed many optimizations on top of FIRe: the overall spaced repetition model not only accounts for implicit "trickle-down" repetitions, but also minimizes the number of reviews by choosing reviews whose implicit repetitions "knock out" other due reviews (like dominos), and calibrates the speed of the spaced repetition process to each individual student on each individual topic (student ability and topic difficulty are competing factors).

In addition to the above, I also developed the following:

- Our gamified features including XP and weekly leaderboards. The XP system is particularly nuanced so that it functions as a reward/penalty system to incentivize student effort. Upon introducing carefully-calibrated XP awards and penalties, most adversarial students' rates of passing learning tasks jumped from under 50% to over 90%. (Non-adversarial students rarely, if ever, experience penalties.)
- Our analytics tools. They allow us to improve our content, without learning standards, to the point that students pass lessons over 99% of the time without remedial intervention.
- Our knowledge graph management tools. They allow us to carry out content revisions quickly and safely in the production database, without requiring a separate staging server.
- Our content development tools. They allow us to produce content many times more efficiently than fully manual content development, while maintaining the same level of quality.
- Our system-wide validations. They run continuously to immediately alert us of any issues relating to the knowledge graph or the decisions of our adaptive learning algorithms.
- The Math Academy Way, a 400+ page deep dive into the literature on the science of learning and talent development, with hundreds of academic citations and relevant quotes pulled out of them.
- The initial version of our knowledge graph visualization.
- (I also wrote hundreds of our initial lessons, and while I'm less involved on the content side nowadays, I still encode lots of domain-expert knowledge into our knowledge graph and do spot checks on all the courses we release. I've also been pulled back onto the content side recently, heavily involved in developing our upcoming ML/CS courses -- especially the CS course, which I'm developing mostly solo.)

All of my work at Math Academy has been the result of heavy collaboration with Jason Roberts. Pretty much every young technical cannon needs a mentor to point them towards a series of progressively larger subproblems leading up to a big unsolved problem that's worth solving. Jason is that mentor for me. We'll talk about a vision for the ultimate math learning system, he'll identify high-leverage problems that feel like they should be possible to solve, and I'll make it happen.

The third stage is after a student has learned some material and done some review on it, they get quizzed on it. Quizzes on Math Academy happen about every 150 minutes of work. We measure work in XP (experience points), where one XP is roughly equivalent to one minute of work for an average student at that level. Quizzes come every two and a half hours, maybe every two and a half hours. This is not like a typical classroom, where you might get a quiz every two weeks at most, or maybe every two months for a student who’s using Math Academy along a class schedule. For a student spending 50 minutes a day on Math Academy, they will get a couple of quizzes a week.

These quizzes are 15-minute quizzes, but they are packed with quite a few questions. In lower grades, you might get 20 questions on a 15-minute quiz. By the time a student enters the quiz, they should be strong enough on the material to pull it out of their brain in a reasonably quick timeframe and start building the level of automaticity they need. In higher-level courses, like calculus, it might be more like six or seven questions for a 15-minute quiz. We calibrate the number of questions in a quiz to the amount of time we expect the questions to take. The idea is that we are always focused on retrieval practice, gradually stripping away reference material, and having students retrieve under time constraints to build automaticity.

Justin: One thing that I want to say is a common reaction, especially from adults using our system, is that they get to a point where they have this real emotional experience of seeing some math on a system that they had tried to learn previously. They were really intimidated by it because previously it did not go well at all, and it just felt out of reach. They were thinking, “I guess I am just a dummy because I don’t understand any of this math.” But when they see it on our system, it’s a totally different feeling. They say, “Wait, that’s all it is? It just comes down to these prerequisites I know. That’s all I was missing. I thought I was dumb, but it turns out I was just missing the prerequisites.”

Then they look at all the time they spent in the past just banging their head on these problems when they could have been filling in their prerequisite knowledge. It gets so much easier to learn. That’s a very common reaction with our adults.

Justin: I should say that when a student is advanced and sitting in a class just rehashing things they’ve already learned, that’s not a good use of time. Every student needs instruction that is appropriate for them. A student doesn’t need to be advanced or even at grade level to benefit from individualized instruction.

I don’t want to turn off people who don’t think of themselves as advanced learners because the benefits of filling in your prerequisite knowledge and having instruction adapted to your pace of learning really benefit all students. Even if a student is below grade level, if they are below grade level just because they have missing knowledge, then we can fill that knowledge up quickly for them. # 元游戏播客 #39：Math Academy 与学习科学
...
这期近两小时的播客是嘉宾 Justin Skycak 关于「严肃提升技能」与「寻找使命」的一次系统阐述。对话从微观的学习科学延伸到宏观的人生战略，核心框架可总结如下：

### 一、微观层面：高效学习的科学原理

Justin 将技能进步归结为一个公式：进步 = 效率 × 总量，两者缺一不可。

- 起步阶段的关键是降低门槛：初学者不必追求完美计划，核心任务是“哄骗自己先动起来”，用最小的行动积累正向反馈，度过最初的枯燥排斥期。外在激励（如金钱下注、社交承诺）在此阶段至关重要。
- 核心学习铁律：

- 主动学习：用最少的时间听讲，90%的时间用于亲自解题实战。
- 间隔重复（「等重训练」）：故意等待记忆衰退后再强行提取，这痛苦的「拉扯动作」才是记忆变强的本质。
- 交错练习：避免集中刷同类题，应混合不同题型练习，训练大脑在不同背景间切换并提取记忆的能力。
- 测试效应：解题时严禁依赖参考资料，必须进行“冷启动”式闭卷提取，参考资料只能作为“健身房保护员”给予最小限度的提示。
- 知识图谱的「广度优先」策略：层层平铺推进，避免在单一单元孤军深入，防止产生虚假的掌握感。
...
Justin 将才能培养分为三个阶段：广泛采样期 → 聚焦过滤期 → 大师级创作期。
...
- 如何寻找使命：没有捷径，必须在各类兴趣上投入海量时间去「广泛采样」，获得切身体感。当技能攀爬到足以俯瞰行业全景时，才能找到自己能为世界做出的独特贡献。
- 职业中期转型策略：不建议情绪化裸辞。
...
- 「手不离石」原则：认准自己要推的「宿命巨石」，时刻警惕被路边看似新奇的偏门难题带偏。
...
- 应对连续打卡中断：主动设置「容错休息日」或直接修炼「不因中断而产生负面情绪」的坦然心态。
...
- 善用社群力量：融入同频社群，大方分享哪怕是起步阶段的微小进步。
...
最后，Justin 指出，一切技能提升的本质就是训练大脑把信息从长期记忆中「强行提取」出来的能力。如果用健身房的镜子审视自己的学习行为，就能一眼看穿自己是在真训练还是在自欺欺人。
...
这期播客是迄今为止对我关于严肃提升技能的想法最全面的 2 小时概述。不仅关于如何高效训练，而且关于如何找到你的使命。不仅关于微观结构，而且关于元游戏（大局策略）。
...
Justin Skycak： 你可以请世界上最顶尖的教练来指导，他也可以为你量身定制最完美的训练动作。但如果你每个月只露面一次、每次仅练 30 分钟，结果会怎样呢？

这其中有两个决定性因素：你的训练效率和你的训练总量。你所能取得的进步，本质上是这两个因素相乘的积。如果其中任何一个数值极低，你都无法取得进步。我们要解决的一方面是效率——竭尽全力让每一次训练都发挥最大的成效。但另一方面，你必须保证稳定的出勤率。否则，你根本无法取得任何实质性的突破。

世上没有什么灵丹妙药，能让你仅凭一次 30 分钟的突击干预，就瞬间精通所有数学，或者突然蜕变成健美冠军和奥运体操选手。这是一场漫长的持久战。你必须持之以恒，而这种「持之以恒」，意味着它要内化为每周打卡数次的日常习惯。你必须沉下心来，有意识、有计划地去提升自己在某个领域的技能。你可能需要每周在上面雷打不动地投入好几个小时，并且合理分摊到好几天里。

学生群体其实可以从很多维度进行划分，但最核心的一个分水岭，在于「主动渴望来上课、求知」的学生，与「纯粹被动应付」的学生。这种学生构成往往会逼得老师不得不妥协，被迫放弃一部分教学效率，仅仅为了把那些本来根本不愿跨进教室的学生生拉硬拽进来。

说回刻意练习——这确实很痛苦，而且体验并不美妙。你必须在主观上极度渴望提升，才能咬牙坚持。如果面对一整个班级，孩子们抱着两种截然不同的心态——一些人渴望在刻意练习中磨炼并...

results.summary:
Hi there, my name is Justin Skycak, I'm the Director of Analytics & Algorithms at Math Academy, I developed all of our quantitative software, and I'd be happy to answer your questions.

1. The AI is more like an expert system that emulates the decisions of an expert tutor with regard to what tasks a student should work on at any given point in time (what should the student learn next, what do they need to review). There's a knowledge graph that encodes structural relationships between thousands of math topics (such as prerequisite relationships, but also other types). And then there's an algorithmic reasoning system that looks at a student's answers, overlays them on the knowledge graph, figures out what the student knows (and how well they know it), and decides what learning tasks are going to move the needle most given their personal knowledge profile. The decision-making is inspired by cognitive learning strategies such as mastery learning, spaced repetition, interleaving, minimizing associative interference.

2. Yes, spaced repetition is a core part of the system. Each student has a personalized spaced repetition schedule that adapts to their performance on each topic, and when choosing what topics a student should review or learn next, we're always trying to implicitly "knock out" as many due reviews as possible to maximize learning efficiency. (For instance, if a student is due for a review on one-step ax=b equations, we can implicitly "knock out" that review by having them learn two-step ax+b=c equations instead.)

From a quantitative standpoint, the spaced repetition model was one of the more challenging (but equally fun) parts to build. You normally think of spaced repetition in the context of independent flashcards, but in a hierarchical body of knowledge like mathematics, it gets really complicated because repetitions on advanced topics should "trickle down" to update the repetition schedules of simpler topics that are implicitly practiced (while being discounted appropriately since these repetitions are often too early to count for full credit towards the next repetition).

Our spaced repetition model not only accounts for implicit "trickle-down" repetitions but also minimizes the number of reviews by choosing reviews whose implicit repetitions "knock out" other due reviews (like dominos), and calibrates the speed of the spaced repetition process to each individual student on each individual topic (student ability and topic difficulty are competing factors).

FYI, the "why not just learn from a Khan Academy / MIT OpenCourseWare / a textbook / etc" question comes up from time to time, so I wrote up a detailed answer here: https://justinmath.com/why-not-just-learn-from-a-textbook/

TLDR: I learned from those kinds of resources myself, and while I came a long way, for the amount of effort I put into learning, I could have gone a lot further if my time were used more efficiently. That's the problem that Math Academy solves.

Just a heads up that there's an explanation for this; I responded to the original comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41556644) but I'll also paste here in case anyone misses it:

1. New tasks are selected only as you complete existing tasks (so if you come back after 2 weeks, you need to complete some existing tasks from 2 weeks ago to get new tasks selected based on your knowledge profile right now).

- XP mechanisms—a standardized representation of “pace” (1 XP is meant to approximate 1 min of work)
- Input/effort-based, (mostly) not output/result-based
- Displays predicted completion time for course based on current pace; also displays how long it would take if you had various other paces, so you can see consequences of change.
- Leaderboards offer another answer to “Is my pace reasonable?” You can see: “OK, this pace is roughly average” or “I’m spending a lot more time on this than most people”.
- Small XP bonuses for 100%-correctness discourage sloppiness
- Interleaves prerequisites from prior courses into queue as dependency graph allows, rather than simply requiring learners to complete everything from prior courses “up front”.
- Novel hierarchical spaced repetition system lowers review burden by marking knowledge implicitly partially reviewed when later lessons make use of it
- Periodic “quizzes” interleave multiple lessons’ content and increase transfer (because student must determine what is being asked)

No sense of what these items are, where they’re coming from in the map of the course, how they relate to each other, etc. Creates emotional disconnect and a feeling of passivity.
- This also makes it difficult to create a coherent narrative arc across the material.
- Explanation is very instructional, mostly lacks discussion of motivation, implication, meaning. Theorems are often presented as things-to-be-learned, rather than things-to-be-understood. A sense of learning a sea of isolated facts, rather than a beautiful and coherent whole.
